clue.text: Time to dispatch leader for us

indicators.note: dispatching the leader means the first letter of the word for time is sent away

parts.note: an hour is a unit of time

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a moment to send their team captain off on the group's behalf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to dispatch leader' takes the H off HOUR. The answer opens the top row's theme: OUR COUNTRY WEE ONE ENGLAND NIL, Northern Ireland's 1-0 win over England in September 2005.
explanation.definitionFit: A possessive meaning belonging to us, the sense of 'for us' in 'our house'.

clue.text: Breaking scoreless deadlock, flanker finally burst through

indicators.note: breaking into the deadlock means the next pieces go inside the pair of noughts

parts.note: a 0-0 draw, two noughts written as two Os
a wing is a player on the flank of a football or rugby side

indicators.note: finally picks out the closing letter of the word burst

explanation.surface: A winger's late surge breaks a goalless stalemate in a football match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking' puts WING plus T (from 'finally burst') inside OO, the 0-0 of a scoreless deadlock.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean because of, as in 'cancelled through illness'.

clue.text: Do nine times the repair work after untimely first effort?

definitions.text: Do nine times the repair work after untimely first effort?

parts.words: Do nine times the repair work after untimely first effort?
parts.note: plays on the proverb that a stitch in time saves nine: miss the timely stitch and the mending must be done over

explanation.surface: Someone who put off a small mend now faces nine times the work.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'a stitch in time saves nine' says a prompt repair saves nine later ones; the clue pictures the stitching having to be done again.
explanation.definitionFit: To stitch a second time is what a late first repair forces.

clue.text: Wilts perhaps when eating first of rhubarb sticks?

indicators.note: eating means the first word swallows the letter that follows

parts.note: Wilts is the short name of Wiltshire, an English county, so it is an example of one

indicators.note: first of picks the opening letter of rhubarb

explanation.surface: Does the rhubarb wilt when it is fed sticks?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wilts' reads as a verb but is Wiltshire, a county in south-west England; 'eating' puts R inside COUNTY. 'The sticks' is slang for rural areas.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The sticks' is informal for remote rural land, away from towns.

clue.text: Sculptor makes perfect sort of hole beneath chamber

indicators.note: in a down answer, beneath puts the second piece below the first

parts.note: a cell is a small room or chamber
a hole in one is the perfect golf hole, written IN plus I for one

explanation.surface: An artist produces a flawless hollow below a room.
explanation.walkthrough: A hole in one is golf's perfect hole; 'one' is the Roman numeral I, giving IN I under CELL. Benvenuto Cellini was a Florentine Renaissance sculptor and goldsmith.
explanation.definitionFit: Benvenuto Cellini, maker of the bronze Perseus in Florence, was a Renaissance sculptor.

clue.text: Ashes holders score after swapping opening pair

indicators.note: swapping the opening pair means the first two letters of the word for score change places

parts.note: runs are what a batsman scores in cricket

explanation.surface: The holders of cricket's Ashes score runs after a change at the top of the order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ashes holders' points to cricket's Ashes series, but the ashes here are a cremation's. Swapping R and U in RUNS gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Vessels used to keep a cremated person's remains.

clue.text: "How things are spoiled with yeast!", interjected

indicators.note: interjected means the extra letter is thrust into the middle of the rearranged letters
spoiled signals that the letters of the following words are messed up into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A baker grumbles that the dough has gone wrong because of the yeast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spoiled' rearranges WITH YEAST to THEWAYTIS, and 'interjected' drops a further I into it. The OCR read the printed I as an exclamation mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A resigned phrase for the present state of affairs, synonymous with 'that's life'.

clue.text: Get zany new Chinese feature with banks

indicators.note: new signals that the letters are made into a fresh word

explanation.surface: An instruction to acquire a quirky novelty from China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges GET ZANY. The definition's 'banks' are a river's.
explanation.definitionFit: The Yangtze is China's longest river, and a river has banks on either side.

clue.text: Doing this little is a relief!

definitions.text: Doing this little is a relief!

parts.words: Doing this little is a relief!
parts.note: reads as a small act bringing comfort; it is the childish word for urinating, which is also Scots for little

explanation.surface: Relieving oneself, even a small amount, feels good.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses run together: a childish word for passing water, and a Scots word for small. The theme row reads OUR COUNTRY WEE ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the bladder sense (a relief) and the small sense (little) are covered by one word.

clue.text: Dab hand with one bit of gauze, almost the last

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: bit of says a single letter is taken from the word gauze
almost the last letter of gauze is the one before its final letter

explanation.surface: An expert applies a scrap of gauze, almost the final piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bit of' and 'almost the last' together pick Z, the letter before the final E of 'gauze'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dab hand and a whizz are both informal words for an expert.

clue.text: As one sees, Sam never covers up

indicators.note: in a down answer, up means the concealed letters are read from bottom to top
covers means the letters lie concealed within the words sees, Sam never

explanation.surface: A remark that Sam never conceals anything, as anyone can see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covers' hides ESSAMNE in 'seES SAM NEver'; 'up' reads it backwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: French for 'in a body', all together, so acting as one.

clue.text: Pub chef oddly keeps fish sauce

indicators.note: keeps means the first pieces hold the fish inside them

parts.note: an inn is a pub
sole is a flatfish

indicators.note: oddly picks the first and third letters of chef

explanation.surface: A pub's chef keeps fish sauce in stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' takes CE from 'chef'; 'keeps' puts SOLE inside INN+CE. 'Sauce' is the impudence sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Sauce in the sense of cheek or impudence, as in 'none of your sauce'.

clue.text: Chief from the east capturing heart of Tadzhik prince

indicators.note: capturing means the turned word takes the middle letter inside it
in an across answer, read from the east means from right to left

parts.note: main means chief or principal

indicators.note: heart of picks the central letter of the seven-letter Tadzhik

explanation.surface: A leader from the east seizes the heart of a Central Asian prince.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from the east' turns MAIN to NIAM; 'capturing' puts Z, the centre of TADZHIK, inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nizam of Hyderabad was the title of the ruling prince of that Indian state.

clue.text: Chivalrous old chap recalled 17 across -a future Mrs Rooney?

indicators.note: recalled means the whole string of pieces is called back, read in reverse

parts.note: NI is the abbreviation for the country entered at 17 across
a WAG, one of the wives and girlfriends of England footballers; Coleen McLoughlin was Wayne Rooney's girlfriend before marrying him

explanation.surface: A knightly figure is reminded of a Belfast girl who might marry a footballer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalled' reverses NI+A+WAG. Sir Gawain is a knight of the Round Table; the setter noted GAWA is also the Green and White Army, Northern Ireland's fans.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Gawain was one of Arthur's knights of the Round Table, models of chivalry.

clue.text: Delights in unusual exercises — bend and stretch briefly

indicators.note: in places the exercise and bend letters within the word for unusual

parts.note: rare means unusual
PT is physical training, exercises
a U-bend is a bend shaped like the letter U

indicators.note: briefly cuts stretch down to its opening letter

explanation.surface: Someone loves unusual workouts of bending and stretching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' reads as an anagram signal but gives RARE; 'in' puts PT and U inside it, and 'briefly' shortens 'stretch' to S.
explanation.definitionFit: Raptures are ecstatic delights, states of intense joy.

clue.text: Dish organist had at regular intervals

indicators.note: at regular intervals picks every second letter across organist had

explanation.surface: A cook reports what the church organist ate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at regular intervals' takes the 2nd, 4th, 6th, 8th and 10th letters of 'oRgAnIsT hAd'.
explanation.definitionFit: Raita is an Indian side dish of yoghurt with cucumber or mint.

clue.text: Crew clutch unusual indoor decoration

indicators.note: clutch means the first word grips the rearranged letters inside it

parts.note: a gang is a crew or team of workers

indicators.note: unusual signals that the letters of indoor are rearranged

explanation.surface: A team grabs an odd piece of interior ornament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges INDOOR to DROONI, and 'clutch' puts it inside GANG.
explanation.definitionFit: Gadrooning is ornamental notched or fluted edging on silver or woodwork.

clue.text: -E-mail infection uncommon, note, very uncommon

indicators.note: uncommon signals the letters of the two words are rearranged into something unusual

parts.note: E is a musical note

explanation.surface: An email virus is rare, a note says, extremely rare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncommon' rearranges EMAIL INFECTION to ONCEINALIFETIM; the note E follows. The blog read the note as ME, but the letter count leaves room only for E.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens only once in a lifetime is extremely rare.

clue.text: Bar substitute from starting complaining about remaining on bench

indicators.note: starting picks the first letter of each of the five words that follow

explanation.surface: A substitute keeps grumbling about being left on the bench.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starting' takes the first letters of 'complaining about remaining on bench'. The 'bar' is a chocolate bar, not a pub or a football crossbar.
explanation.definitionFit: Carob is a sweet bean powder used in place of chocolate in confectionery bars.

clue.text: Eleven of Windsor Park's 30 deer ran wild, chasing Pole

indicators.note: chasing means the following letters come after the pole, in an across answer

parts.note: North is one of the two poles

indicators.note: wild signals that the letters of nil, deer and ran are rearranged

parts.note: the answer to 30 across, which means a duck or zero

explanation.surface: Deer stampede through a Belfast football ground, chasing a Polish visitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges NIL (30 across) with DEER RAN, and 'chasing' sets that after NORTH. Windsor Park in Belfast is the home ground of the Northern Ireland football team.
explanation.definitionFit: The national football team plays its home matches at Windsor Park, Belfast, so it is that ground's eleven.

clue.text: He's not South American and not old-about ten

indicators.note: about means the first pieces go round the number that follows

parts.note: nor means and not

explanation.surface: A man denies being South American or elderly, and is around ten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts TEN inside NOR+O. A norteño is a northern Mexican, so a North American.
explanation.definitionFit: A norteño is a person from northern Mexico, which is in North America, not South.

clue.text: Male rivals holding hands swallow black poisonous plant

annotationWithheld.why: Male rivals holding hands swallow black poisonous plant: HE + NE (bridge rivals) round B+AN needs 'hands' to give AN, which no sense supports; no parse found
annotationWithheld.clue: Male rivals holding hands swallow black poisonous plant

clue.text: A shade intrusive in ephemeral dalliance

indicators.note: intrusive in means the answer pushes its way inside the words ephemeral dalliance

explanation.surface: A ghost intrudes on a brief love affair.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside 'ephEMERAL Dalliance'. 'Shade' looks like a ghost but is a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Emerald is a bright green colour, a shade named after the gemstone.

clue.text: Completed female part of 17 across? Yes and no

definitions.text: part of 17 across? Yes and no

parts.note: done means completed or finished
gal is an informal word for a girl or woman

explanation.surface: A finished woman wonders whether she belongs to a region.
explanation.walkthrough: Donegal is in the province of Ulster but in the Republic of Ireland, not in Northern Ireland: hence 'Yes and no'.
explanation.definitionFit: The county is in historic Ulster but outside the UK province across the border.

clue.text: Christmas Cards may have this person posing on TV

definitions.meaning: Christmas cards often show a red-breasted bird sitting on a branch or snow
Anne ... posed the questions on the TV quiz The Weakest Link

explanation.walkthrough: Split as ROBIN'S ON: a robin is a stock Christmas card picture in Britain. Anne Robinson hosted The Weakest Link, so she 'poses' questions.
explanation.definitionFit: A card has a robin on it; and Anne Robinson put questions as a television quizmaster.

clue.text: Hit school broadcast on 7th of September

indicators.note: in an across answer, on means the next piece follows the letter
7th of picks the seventh letter of the word September
broadcast means the school's name is heard as a word that sounds like it

parts.note: Eton is the English public school near Windsor

explanation.surface: A school is struck in a broadcast on 7 September.
explanation.walkthrough: The seventh letter of 'September' is B. ETON spoken sounds like EATEN. 7 September 2005 was the date of Northern Ireland's win over England.
explanation.definitionFit: Beaten means struck repeatedly, the past participle of hit in its battering sense.

clue.text: Old Greek tragedian, having no paper, departs

indicators.note: having no means the following pieces are taken out of the word tragedian

parts.note: rag is a disparaging word for a newspaper
D is the timetable abbreviation for departs

explanation.surface: An ancient tragedian, without his script, leaves the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having no' removes RAG and D from TRAGEDIAN. 'Tragedian' looks like the definition, but it is the fodder; the Teian poet Anacreon came from Teos.
explanation.definitionFit: A Teian was a native of Teos, an ancient Greek city in Ionia.

clue.text: One who built fortification from nothing

parts.note: of can mean from, as in 'a man of Kent'
FA is short for sweet FA, slang for nothing at all

explanation.surface: A builder made his defences out of nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweet FA is British slang for nothing at all. Offa, an eighth-century king of Mercia, built Offa's Dyke along the Welsh border.
explanation.definitionFit: King Offa of Mercia is credited with the earthwork Offa's Dyke on the Welsh border.

clue.text: Innovative half back is musical

indicators.note: back means the picked letters are read in the opposite direction
half takes the latter five letters of the ten-letter word innovative

explanation.surface: A creative half-back plays football with style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' keeps ATIVE from 'innovative' and 'back' reverses it. A half-back is a football position, which hides the device.
explanation.definitionFit: Evita is the Lloyd Webber and Rice stage musical about Eva Perón.

clue.text: Increasingly up to Cockney to speak of passion

indicators.note: to speak means the word is said and the sound gives the answer

parts.note: higher means increasingly up, and a Cockney drops the H

explanation.surface: Someone climbs higher while a Londoner talks heatedly.
explanation.walkthrough: Higher is 'increasingly up'; a Cockney drops the H, and 'igher said in a non-rhotic accent sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ire is anger, a strong passion.

clue.text: Adding spark to obscure Florida dynasty

parts.note: in can mean understood only by a few, as in an in-joke
Fla is the abbreviation for the US state of Florida
the Ming were a Chinese dynasty

explanation.surface: Lighting up an obscure family that once ruled Florida.
explanation.walkthrough: IN in the sense of an in-joke, private to a few, is 'obscure'. The answer means firing up, as with a spark.
explanation.definitionFit: To set alight or stir up passion is to put a spark to something.

clue.text: Popping pills whole?

parts.note: being on drugs means taking them, as when popping pills
E is slang for an ecstasy pill

explanation.surface: Is swallowing tablets whole the right way?
explanation.walkthrough: 'On E' is slang for being on ecstasy, so 'popping pills'. The theme row reads WEE ONE: Northern Ireland won 1-0.
explanation.definitionFit: One means a single unit, all together, a complete whole.

clue.text: Cricket team went in the middle with sweater

indicators.note: in the middle picks the central pair of letters of the word went

parts.note: a sweat gland is a gland that makes you sweat

explanation.surface: A cricket team went out with a pullover at the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sweater' looks like a jumper but is a sweat gland, one that sweats. The theme's bottom row reads ENGLAND NIL.
explanation.definitionFit: England fields a national cricket team, as well as the football side beaten in the theme.

clue.text: A duck taking 17 across lake

parts.note: NI is the abbreviation for the country entered at 17 across
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A duck carrying a lake across.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck is cricket's word for a score of zero; 'taking' joins NI and L.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a duck is a score of nothing, the same as zero in football.
